quote: The central bank does not have access to customer data and does not have responsibility for AML/KYC/CTF, but through its own roles it has access to aggregated overviews of circulation, holdings, and transaction activity on the ledger.
modality: unconditional within the tested design; identity link possible only via banks or court orders (see F9)
justification: In the most recent design material the central bank holds a pseudonymous ledger and no identity mapping. The tested retail sandbox states this (doc 7 p. 11; doc 6 p. 12), and the 2026 rough-draft design features frame it as inability, not non-use: 'it should not be possible for the central bank to monitor' (doc 6 p. 16). No body has adopted a design: the Board found a CBDC 'currently not warranted' (doc 6 p. 2), and doc 6 p. 15 calls the design list a rough draft. The value is therefore carried with claim_status tested and evidence_state partial, never as a commitment. Earlier options with CB linkage, the closed-account variants (doc 2 p. 32; doc 4 p. 26), were alternatives that do not appear in the 2026 drafts. The pseudonymity caveat (doc 7 p. 11) belongs to F9.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 26: In a closed account solution, any holdings will be linked to an identifiable person. Norges Bank can control the release of information

quote: Banks are responsible for customer onboarding and for linking customers to ledger addresses that are registered in the banks’ own account registers.
justification: Under §6.5 all three premises must be documented for the same design version. For the 2026 tested design only premise (i) is documented: banks hold the address-to-person mapping (doc 7 p. 9; doc 7 p. 11; doc 6 p. 12). Routine bank visibility of transaction records (ii) and linkage in the same mode (iii) are not stated. Doc 6 p. 12 names banks only as a possible linking source. The 2021 statement that third parties must identify transferors and transferees (doc 4 p. 25) is conditional on a different, earlier design option and cannot supply premises for the 2026 design. A customer relationship alone (doc 6 p. 16) is insufficient.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 25: user interfaces must be able to access information identifying CBDC

quote: Know Your Customer (KYC), Countering the Financing of Terrorism (CTF) and Anti Money Laundering (AML) requirements for CBDC would be the same as for other payment services.
justification: The F3 trap applies: a 'same rules' statement is via_PSP only if the PSP is named as the data holder, and here it is not. The latest documents leave the holder open. Doc 6 p. 22 says 'it must be clarified who is to be responsible for transaction monitoring', and doc 5 p. 15 says this 'must be resolved through legislative amendments'. Earlier routes were options in other design versions: STRs by third parties (doc 4 p. 24) and possible use of register information by tax and supervisory authorities (doc 4 p. 43). Because these point to different routes and are not carried into the current drafts, the value is n/d.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 24: Customer due diligence encompasses ... identity checks when on-boarding users, transaction checks and the reporting of suspicious transactions.

quote: A design requirement for any CBDC solution should be that it is capable of functioning independently of bank payment systems, and of implementing “offline” payments for a certain period.
justification: Offline functionality appears only as a desirable or required characteristic. Its privacy and synchronisation behaviour are not described (doc 3 p. 4; doc 4 p. 9; doc 4 p. 37), so the contract rule 'offline without a privacy description → unknown' applies. The only privacy-describing passage, 'anonymous pre-paid cards' (doc 4 p. 26), is an option without synchronisation behaviour. Doc 4 p. 42 suggests anonymity may be unavailable offline. No offline mode was adopted, and none is mentioned in the 2026 design features.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 26: Since this solution will also feature local storage, anonymous pre-paid cards can ensure anonymity within permitted quantitative limits.

quote: Since this solution will also feature local storage, anonymous pre-paid cards can ensure anonymity within permitted quantitative limits.
modality: conditional: closed account solution with local storage
justification: Low-identification routes appear only as considered options with unspecified limits (doc 2 p. 28; doc 4 p. 26; doc 4 p. 29), so no adopted mode exists. The §6.6a inference to 'no' is blocked because other project documents do mention lower-identification tiers. The 2026 draft only routes acquisition through the user's own bank account (doc 6 p. 16), which is silence about other routes, not an explicit all-routes identification requirement. Hence n/d rather than no.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p. 16: It must be straightforward for the public to acquire retail CBDC through online and mobile banking services and ATMs by debiting their own bank accounts.

quote: KYC and AML checks of CBDC users would have to be performed by banks or other market participants that offer wallets for CBDC storage and transactions to their customers.
modality: conditional: if issued; rough-draft design feature
justification: Every design version requires KYC by banks or third parties at onboarding: doc 2 p. 27, doc 4 p. 43, doc 5 p. 14 (CDD rests with banks), and bank-approved addresses in the tested sandbox (doc 7 p. 9). The 2026 list is explicitly a rough draft (doc 6 p. 15), so the value is not an adopted commitment and the evidence is partial. Per contract, F8 is descriptive and not a premise for F2.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 29: In principle, holdings stored in wallets do not have to be linked with an identity.

quote: If the ledger address of an end-user can be linked to an identity – either through banks, court orders, technical leaks or data collocation – any participant with read access to the ledger would be able to view the entire transaction history related to this address.
actor: banks / courts (via court orders) / any participant with read access
modality: conditional: address-identity link via banks, court orders, leaks or data collocation
justification: The tested pseudonymous Besu design allows retrospective attribution of the full transaction history once an address is linked to an identity, including via banks or court orders (doc 6 p. 12; doc 7 p. 11). This is a tested finding, not an adopted design. Earlier options also foresee identity linkage for large or suspicious transactions (doc 4 p. 26) and key-based disclosure under specified procedures (doc 4 p. 40). The cell is descriptive and qualifies F1 = no.

quote: CBDC should not be programmable money, and programmability, if implemented, should be at the payment service level.
justification: The latest design statement rejects programmable money and adds a principle of unrestricted usability (doc 6 p. 17). This follows the 2021 working-group conclusion favouring limited programming functionality (doc 4 p. 47). The 2021 discussion of social-support funds restricted to specific uses (doc 4 p. 43) was an option. The confiscation function in the 2023 prototype (doc 5 p. 8) is tested, with no stated purpose beyond AML. The value is a rough-draft option, not adopted.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 43: CBDC units used to pay various forms of social support may be programmed to be usable only in certain circumstances

quote: When Norges Bank launched its CBDC project, the primary motivation was the central bank’s desire to facilitate a secure and efficient payment system without negatively impacting the other objectives laid down in the Central Bank Act.
justification: A secure and efficient payment system is declared repeatedly as the aim (doc 2 p. 5; doc 5 p. 3; doc 6 p. 2). Strategy 25 frames it as keeping NOK a 'safe, efficient and attractive means of payment' (doc 5 p. 15; doc 7 p. 2). Doc 1 p. 33 rejects only the cost argument, not the payment-system objective.
counter_evidence: doc 1 p. 33: The working group has therefore concluded that the cost argument for introducing a CBDC in Norway is not decisive.

quote: Introducing a retail CBDC is not a suitable measure for financial inclusion in Norway.
justification: Inclusion is explicitly considered and rejected as a CBDC rationale, both in 2026 and earlier (doc 2 p. 13). The accessibility remarks are design requirements (doc 4 p. 15) or cash attributes (doc 1 p. 18), not declared objectives. 'No' reflects an explicit rejection, not mere absence.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 15: Any CBDC should therefore have an IT architecture that allows Norges Bank or third parties to offer simple, accessible solutions.

quote: A CBDC can secure technical autonomy from ordinary payment systems and national control. The latter may become particularly important if other payment infrastructure is relocated outside Norway’s borders
modality: conditional: if infrastructure is relocated abroad
justification: National control over the payment system is a recurring, conditional objective (doc 4 p. 4; doc 5 p. 6; doc 6 p. 7; doc 6 p. 9). The monetary-policy-instrument motive is rejected (doc 5 p. 13; doc 1 p. 20), and the risk of currency substitution is judged minor (doc 5 p. 7). Because the sovereignty motive remains a declared conditional rationale, the flag is yes but partial.
counter_evidence: doc 5 p. 13: This discussion draws the overall conclusion that CBDC should not primarily be seen as a monetary policy instrument

quote: function as an independent back-up solution if ordinary electronic payment solutions fail or confidence in the banking system weakens substantially.
justification: Falling cash usage and contingency or back-up are declared throughout. Norges Bank states that its research is motivated by low and falling cash usage (doc 4 p. 4), and contingency recurs as a purpose (doc 2 p. 5; doc 5 p. 3; doc 6 p. 2; doc 6 p. 5). The 2026 judgement that contingency is not currently decisive (doc 6 p. 5) assesses the objective but does not withdraw it as stated.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p. 5: contingency considerations do not at present provide a decisive argument for

quote: CBDC to make it easy to trace the origin of funds and to facilitate ongoing taxation.
justification: The flag requires an objective explicitly declared by the institution. The only finding reports the views of other authorities the working group met, not an objective of Norges Bank. AML compliance statements (doc 6 p. 16) are design requirements. The objective is therefore not documented in the checked sources.

quote: Norges Bank has placed particular emphasis on whether the introduction of a CBDC could promote innovation in payment services and whether it would be a suitable instrument to strengthen contingency arrangements in Norway's payment system.
justification: Innovation and competition are stated purposes. Examples include 'one of its purposes will be to foster competition' (doc 2 p. 32), allowing third parties to innovate (doc 4 p. 27), and meeting competition from bigtechs and stablecoins (doc 5 p. 7). The 2026 conclusion that a CBDC is not appropriate now for promoting innovation (doc 6 p. 5) evaluates the objective rather than denying it was declared.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p. 5: Introducing a retail CBDC is not an appropriate measure at this stage to promote innovation that enhances effective and secure payment services.

quote: When Norges Bank launched its CBDC project, the primary motivation was the central bank’s desire to facilitate a secure and efficient payment system without negatively impacting the other objectives laid down in the Central Bank Act.
justification: An explicit ranking names the payment system as primary. Doc 5 p. 13 confirms it: the argument 'should primarily be linked to the payment system'. The 2018 preface named confidence in money as primary (doc 1 p. 4); later statements on the same matter replace it. Other passages list purposes without ranking (doc 2 p. 6; doc 4 p. 5), and doc 6 p. 5 gives joint emphasis to innovation and contingency as assessment criteria. These are listings or emphases, not a ranking that overrides the explicit 'primary'. The evidence is kept partial because of these competing listings.
counter_evidence: doc 6 p. 5: Norges Bank has placed particular emphasis on whether the introduction of a CBDC could promote innovation in payment services and ... contingency arrangements

quote: the primary motivation was the central bank’s desire to facilitate a secure and efficient payment system
justification: The ranking is documented in doc 4 p. 63 and repeated in doc 5 p. 13 ('primarily linked to the payment system'). The 2018 primary purpose, 'confidence in money and the monetary system' (doc 1 p. 4), is the earlier ranking replaced by these statements.
counter_evidence: doc 1 p. 4: The primary purpose of a CBDC is to ensure confidence in money and the monetary system.

quote: The sandbox solution in this test case is based on Hyperledger Besu, which is a permissioned ledger compatible with the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
justification: Two platforms were tested for the retail core: Hyperledger Besu in 2026 and a private/closed Ethereum network in 2023 (doc 5 p. 8). Per the F12 rule, PoC platforms are claim_status tested, never adopted. The 2026 rough-draft design leans to blockchain and a private ledger 'at least initially' (doc 6 p. 17; doc 6 p. 19), but these are options, and the public-versus-private choice is explicitly still to be decided (doc 6 p. 19). Earlier reports were explicitly undecided (doc 5 p. 10; doc 4 p. 49).
counter_evidence: doc 6 p. 19: Should Norges Bank issue a CBDC solution on a ledger, the Bank must decide whether this ledger should be public or private.
